newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia car market coping with end of ex-Yugo wars.
newsitem.headline: Croatia car market coping with end of ex-Yugo wars.

text.p: The wars in former Yugoslavia destroyed many of Croatia's cars and left many people without money to replace them, but demand is strong and the country's car market is expected to soar at the turn of the century.

Years of fighting destroyed many of the one million vehicles that were on Croatian roads in 1991 while leaving many people unable to afford a new car, automakers said at a motor show that opened here on Monday.

"A lot of people want cars here, but there's not a lot of money to buy them," Martin Hobel, a sales manager for Croatia for Japanese automaker Suzuki Motor Corp , said at Zagreb's sixth annual car show, which runs through April 13.
Nevertheless, many automakers expect the market to soar above 50,000 units at the turn of the century from 21,179 units last year.
And the Croatian government has given sales a boost this year by granting war veterans partial or full exemptions on all taxes on a car's base price, amounting to discounts as high as 45 percent.
"War veterans will be 70 percent of our customers," Antun Lulic, managing director of the Adriatic Automobile Corp, the Croatian importer for U.S. automaker Ford Motor Co, said.
Lulic estimated that 300,000 people are eligible for the tax break, but other automakers said veterans could number over 400,000.

Sales might rise even higher if dealers could stop losing business to neighbouring Hungary, where cash-strapped Croatians have been flocking to buy cars at prices sometimes 1,000 marks to 1,500 marks (($600 to $900) below the market rates in Croatia, automakers said.
Prices on mid-sized family cars are attractive in Hungary because these models are built there by Suzuki and German automaker Adam Opel AG, a division of U.S. automaker General Motors Corp.
Hungary's overall market has become fairly cheap because many car importers there have dropped their prices to compete with Opel and Suzuki.
In 1996, Croatians imported an estimated 5,000 cars from Hungary, mainly Ford Escorts and Hungarian-built Opel Astras and Suzuki Swifts.
"If people find that they can save 1,000 marks, they will cross the border," Lulic said. "It's a lot of money for them."

Croatian imports of these cars, which are deemed used vehicles because they are not sold initially in the country, boosted the used car market to an estimated 25,000 units -- bigger than the new car market.
"The problem is that anyone in Croatia can import a car," said Eugen Sinicic, a salesman for Euroline DD, the importer in Croatia for German automaker Mercedes-Benz AG.
The lack of attractive finance options also has depressed new car sales, as interest rates to lease or buy cars on credit vary between 15 and 20 percent.
"All of our passenger cars are sold for cash," Sinicic said. "Everything is paid before the car is delivered. There are no possibilities for credit."
But South Korean conglomerate Daewoo Group, the most aggressive investor in the auto industry in central and eastern Europe, said it planned to shake up the Croatia market.

"In January, we started selling cars on credit with down-payments of zero percent to 30 percent," Joon-Seo Lee, director of Daewoo's importer in Croatia, told Reuters. "It's the most attractive package in Croatia."

Daewoo, also a large bank operator, is financing the sales itself, a big advantage over most car importers in Croatia, who must rely on the less favourable credit terms available at banks and leasing institutions.
"Over 90 percent of our sales are on credit, and 90 percent of these sales are without a down-payment," Lee added.
"We know it's a risky strategy, but this market is dominated by German brands, and we can't simply follow the others if we want to gain market share." ($ = 1.685 German Marks)
